articles.title: A maintainer's guide to reviewing AI-written pull requests
articles.excerpt: Open-source maintainers have always had to separate noisy pull requests from useful ones. An AI coding assistant can now produce a tidy diff, a confident description, and even tests — and still invent…
articles.body: Open-source maintainers have always had to separate noisy pull requests from useful ones. An AI coding assistant can now produce a tidy diff, a confident description, and even tests — and still invent an API that is not in your tree, ignore nearby conventions, or "fix" something that was never broken. This is not an argument against AI-assisted work. Careful contributors often use an assistant as a drafting tool, then verify the output against the real codebase and stand behind the change. The job is to tell those pull requests apart from ones that were generated, pasted, and opened without that care — quickly, consistently, and without shaming anyone.
articles.author: EGD PR Triage

articles.title: Postgres Evidence Retention in 2026: Audit Logs for E-commerce Product Retrieval
articles.excerpt: Short answer: for e-commerce product search, choose a retrieval architecture that records the decision inputs, candidate identities, policy version, and cited evidence in one append-only audit event;…
articles.body: Short answer: for e-commerce product search, choose a retrieval architecture that records the decision inputs, candidate identities, policy version, and cited evidence in one append-only audit event; don't treat the final answer or a general application log as an adequate record. In a B2B SaaS internal knowledge-base bot, that boundary lets an operator explain which catalog material was eligible without retaining every product description or employee question forever. The key trade-off is evidence versus exposure. Logging too little makes a grounded answer impossible to investigate. Logging raw queries, chunks, and generated text by default creates a second content store with its own access and retention burden.
articles.author: MitchellCross2134

articles.title: TryHackMe – Corridor: Finding the Hidden Door Through IDOR
articles.excerpt: 1. Introduction In this write-up, I will document my experience completing the Corridor room on TryHackMe, focusing on identifying and exploiting an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerabili…
articles.body: 1. Introduction In this write-up, I will document my experience completing the Corridor room on TryHackMe , focusing on identifying and exploiting an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) vulnerability. At first glance, the challenge looks relatively simple. The web application presents a corridor containing multiple doors. Each door represents a different location, and clicking on one redirects us to another URL. However, something interesting caught my attention: the URLs contained long hexadecimal strings that looked like MD5 hashes. Instead of randomly clicking through every door, I decided to investigate how these URLs were generated and whether the application was using predictable identifiers behind the scenes.

I found an alternative that may save you 15 minutes. Road construction has also been reported ahead." During the journey, the vehicle observes traffic signals, pedestrians, cyclists, road signs, lane markings, and surrounding vehicles. It analyzes road conditions, follows validated driving policies, and communicates with passengers through a natural voice interface. But what if it could do even more? What if it could learn from approved driving experiences, identify recurring road risks, forecast maintenance requirements, and receive secure software improvements over time?

articles.excerpt: We run Correctover — an independent decision table for agent authorization: whether a delegated action exceeds the authorization actually granted, parameter by parameter, not tool by tool. Our verifie…
articles.body: We run Correctover — an independent decision table for agent authorization: whether a delegated action exceeds the authorization actually granted, parameter by parameter, not tool by tool. Our verifier has judged 28 push runs, caught and blocked 5, and every number is recomputable from the GitHub Actions API. Yesterday we published it as a GitHub Action, read our own README one more time — and found the reference line we'd written told people to pin @main , which GitHub Actions cannot resolve. The first failure the tool caught when pointed at ourselves was ours.

articles.title: Lessons From AI Products That Shut Down
articles.excerpt: Originally published on OKAIHub. Products rarely die on launch day. They fade: a busy first week, a quiet second month, a decision to stop paying for infrastructure three months after that. The reason…
articles.body: Originally published on OKAIHub . Products rarely die on launch day. They fade: a busy first week, a quiet second month, a decision to stop paying for infrastructure three months after that. The reasons differ in each case, but a handful of patterns repeat often enough to recognise early — and early is the only time they are cheap to fix. What this is not: There is no public ledger of why a small tool closed, and guessing at a founder's private reasons is not analysis. What follows are failure modes you can observe in your own product, with checks you can run this week rather than stories about companies you cannot verify. Lesson one: a spike is not a business A good launch produces a graph with a tall left edge and a long tail that drops toward zero. That shape is normal.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
articles.body: On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials. They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 star cluster . The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA. It also included figures of a human, the solar system and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

articles.title: Relive Starship’s historic Flight 15 with our best photos from launch and ‘Mechazilla’ tower catch
articles.excerpt: See the most epic photos from SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight and historic launch tower catch.
articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX has officially wrapped up the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket, successfully catching the vehicle's upper stage for the first time. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX's Starbase facility here in South Texas on Friday (Nov. 13). The mission was billed as the first to bring both of Starship's stages, the Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage, back to the launch site for recovery. And, while SpaceX was forced to divert Super Heavy's return to an off-shore splashdown (and explosion), the upper stage managed to survive its 22-hour jaunt in orbit and plunge through the atmosphere for a picture-perfect catch by the launch tower back at Starbase.

articles.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
articles.excerpt: Just a day after SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship megarocket back at the launch pad for the first time ever, Elon Musk told us that the spacecraft will get even bigger.
articles.body: As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big. The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower. It was a huge moment for SpaceX , bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship. "Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15).
